info.bio:
El año 1984, y tras su partida del grupo The Clash, el guitarrista Mick Jones funda Big Audio Dynamite, junto a Don Letts, Dan Donovan, Leo Williams y Greg Roberts. En una extraña mezcla de ska, pop, reggae, dub y dance, lanzó a los ránkings ingleses y norteamericanos singles como "Kool-Aid" y "E=MC2".
A pesar de algunos cambios en su formación y de nombre (Big Audio Dynamite II, Big Audio) se mantuvo activo hasta 1998.

scenes.name: Pop británico de los ochenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Junto al synth-pop, otros grupos trabajan la atmósfera y acuñan un estilo apagado y melódico que revisa el concepto de pop: Young Marble Giants y Raincoats (proto lo-fi), Felt, Talk Talk (Spirit Of Eden, pionero del slo-core). El revival pop (Everything But The Girl, Sade, Scritti Politti, Prefab Sprout, Style Council, Simply Red); Escocia (Orange Juice, Josef K, Aztec Camera, Blue Nile, el «anorak pop» de los Vaselines) e Irlanda; en Inglaterra, los Smiths (el antídoto del punk, como los Beatles lo fueron del rock'n'roll), Wedding Present, Woodentops, Primitives, Waterboys, Big Audio Dynamite; Roxette y los Sugarcubes de Björk.

podcast.title: Boost from Levi's Commercial (1991)
podcast.body: Big Audio Dynamite, Mick Jones's post-Clash project, received a significant boost in promotion due to its association with The Clash's "Should I Stay or Should I Go" being licensed for a 1991 Levi's commercial. This tie-in contributed to renewed interest in Jones's current work. "Big Audio Dynamite got a big push."

podcast.title: "Sample Crazy" Approach (Year not specified)
podcast.body: After Mick Jones was "kicked out of the clash," he formed Big Audio Dynamite and became intensely focused on using sampling technology. The band's sound was characterized by extensive use of samples, reflecting Jones's innovative approach to music creation with this new technology. "After he was kicked out of the clash, he formed a new band called Big Audio Dynamite, and he went sample crazy."

podcast.title: Formation After Clash Disbandment
podcast.body: After The Clash folded following the dismal reception of *Cut the Crap*, Mick Jones went on to form Big Audio Dynamite. This new band had "a good run in the late 80s and early 90s," establishing Mick Jones's musical career post-Clash.

xref.title: Firing of Mick Jones (September 1, 1983) – Manager-Engineered Split That Destroyed the Band
xref.body: Manager Bernie Rhodes had spent years pitting Joe Strummer against Mick Jones, encouraging Joe to fire him. On September 1, 1983, Mick Jones's departure was announced in a formal "Clash Communiqué" stating he had "drifted apart from the original idea of the Clash." The resulting lineup recorded the critically panned *Cut the Crap* (1985), featuring two new members, after which the Clash simply dissolved with no official announcement. Mick Jones went on to major success with Big Audio Dynamite, while Strummer spent over a decade in record-company limbo and never again achieved the stature he had with the Clash. "Firing Mick Jones? Terrible. Joe Strummer thought he knew better than Mick, and he ended up paying for it."

xref.title: Association with The Clash
xref.body: Don Letts was a confidant and friend to both the Sex Pistols and The Clash, later becoming a member of Big Audio Dynamite alongside his Clash bandmate, Mick Jones. "Don Letts, a confidant and friend of both the sex pistols and the clash... And later on, Don would become a member of Big Audio Dynamite with this clash buddy, Mick Jones."

xref.body: Mick Jones was "kicked out of the Clash." Following his departure, he went on to form a new band called Big Audio Dynamite, where he extensively utilized sampling technology. xref.title: Pioneer DJ in Early Punk Scene
xref.body: Don Letts, a member of Big Audio Dynamite with Mick Jones of The Clash, was deeply involved in the early punk scene as a DJ. He played dub and reggae records in clubs, introducing these new genres and sounds to the pioneers of the punk era, marking a significant first in musical cross-pollination. "And he got involved in the early punk scene as a DJ spinning dub and reggae records in clubs, introducing that music to pioneers in the punk era to New genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Clash Career of Mick Jones
xref.body: After being expelled from The Clash, Mick Jones formed the group Big Audio Dynamite, which went on to have a massive hit single with "E = MC²" in 1985 and 1986. This new band's success was largely due to its innovative use of sampling. "That's what became of Mick Jones after he was kicked out of the clash."
